lead.headline: NZ's Venture-Backed Tech Firms Now Worth $133 Billion — But Who's Cashing In?
lead.byline: National · a nationwide tally of unicorns raises the question of what regions outside the big cities actually get from the boom
lead.brief:
New Zealand's technology sector has received some unusually good news: a new report by global data platform Dealroom and NZ Growth Capital Partners estimates the combined enterprise value of New Zealand's venture-backed companies at NZ$133 billion. The report identifies more than 400 firms, including eight "unicorns" that have reached a valuation or exit of more than US$1 billion.

Two of those firms have gone further still: two of these are "decacorns" valued at more than US$10 billion — aerospace firm Rocket Lab and global financial services provider FNZ. Relative to peer innovation economies, New Zealand generates unusually high enterprise value relative to the venture capital invested, an impressive result for a country of New Zealand's size.

But it also prompts a question many local observers will be asking: is New Zealand as good at retaining the wider economic benefits of successful technology companies as it is at creating them? That framing points to the real debate behind the numbers: value creation at this scale hasn't necessarily translated into broad-based national benefit, raising questions about where the gains actually land.
lead.lens:
Hawke's Bay isn't as absent from this story as a national tally might suggest. One of the two firms Dealroom and NZ Growth Capital Partners count as a New Zealand decacorn already operates on the Bay's doorstep. Rocket Lab's first rocket lifted off in May 2017 from its launch pad in Hawke's Bay, and the company has since grown into a major space business built around its 18-metre Electron rocket. The Wairoa District coastline is home to Rocket Lab's Launch Complex 1, the world's first and only private orbital launch site. Rocket Lab's Mahia operations have generated dozens of local jobs in engineering, launch-pad work, logistics and administrative support, alongside a network of more than 300 local suppliers. Launch nights still draw locals and visitors to the official viewing site near Morere Lodge, at the end of Blucks Pit Road in Nūhaka.

So the honest local reading of this report isn't that Hawke's Bay has no stake in the country's tech wealth — it's that hosting the infrastructure and hosting the value are two different things. Rocket Lab became a publicly listed company on the US stock market in 2021, and the enterprise value Dealroom is now measuring sits overwhelmingly with shareholders and head-office functions well beyond Wairoa. The rockets go up from Mahia; the equity, the listing proceeds and most of the highest-value jobs sit elsewhere. That's the same tension the national report raises, already playing out locally. Councils and regional economic agencies don't need to chase a Rocket Lab of their own — the Bay already hosts part of one. The more useful question is whether Wairoa and the wider region are capturing a fair share of the value that a decacorn's actual launch pad generates, in supplier contracts, skills pipelines and the tourism economy that has grown up around watching Electron lift off, rather than simply providing the view.

stories.headline: 619 participants, including 60 rangatahi, build 'AI for good' projects in nationwide challenge heading to Wellington summit
stories.brief: A nationwide push to get young New Zealanders building practical AI tools has drawn 619 participants, including 60 rangatahi, working alongside 114 mentors and 41 industry judges. Nine venue-winning teams now go through to national judging, with four finalists set to pitch at the Aotearoa AI Summit at Tākina, Wellington, on 8–9 September for the 2026 TAIAO Prize.
body: Tech New Zealand's newsletter reports that <cite></cite> from Dunedin to Auckland, 619 participants, including 60 rangatahi, alongside 114 mentors and 41 industry judges joined forces to build AI for good.
<cite></cite> Over two days, teams developed practical AI solutions for challenges including food insecurity, digital accessibility, education, employment and kaitiakitanga.

<cite></cite> The nine venue-winning teams now progress to national judging, with four finalists set to pitch at the Aotearoa AI Summit at Tākina, Wellington, on 8–9 September, and the Summit audience will vote for the 2026 TAIAO Prize winner.

The same newsletter round-up covers other current Tech New Zealand activity. It notes that its Digital Trust Hui Taumata 2026 brought together leaders from government, industry and communities to explore a shared goal of universal trust, with speakers highlighting the need for people-first digital identity, open and interoperable systems, and governance reflecting community needs, and practical use cases discussed from age verification and payments to employment and public services.

Tech New Zealand also used the update to launch a new national community, Quantum & Photonics New Zealand, describing it as bringing together the people and organisations shaping Aotearoa New Zealand's next generation of advanced technologies, alongside news that DataCentres New Zealand has launched an industry-led strategy for the data centre and AI infrastructure the country needs for productivity, resilience and future growth. It also flagged that ShadowTech26 was continuing that week, giving more than 1,500 students across nine locations a first-hand look at technology careers through Tech Women's programme connecting Year 9–11 students with technology workplaces.
stories.lens: This is a genuinely national story rather than a Hawke's Bay one — the newsletter names venues only as running 'from Dunedin to Auckland', with no mention of a Hawke's Bay leg, so it would be dishonest to claim direct local involvement this time. What it does hand the Bay is a template and a deadline: a youth-facing, mentor-heavy AI challenge that pairs rangatahi with industry judges to solve real problems like food insecurity and education — exactly the kind of framing that could suit a region with a strong horticulture and growing sector and a polytechnic like EIT already teaching technology. The concrete, low-risk move for the region is to start asking Tech New Zealand directly what it would take to host or feed a venue into a future round, and for local firms with any AI capability to ask about joining the mentor or judging pool rather than only reading about other regions doing it after the fact. Sending even a small watching brief to the Aotearoa AI Summit in Wellington on 8–9 September, where the TAIAO Prize finalists pitch, would let Hawke's Bay people see firsthand what a winning 'AI for good' project actually looks like before the region decides whether — and how — to try to bring any version of the model home.

stories.headline: Wellington AI startup Sterling raises $3.8m to build an 'autopilot' for finance teams
stories.brief: Wellington-based artificial intelligence startup Sterling has raised $3.8 million in one of the larger seed funding rounds seen recently in New Zealand's tech sector, just 10 months after it was founded. The round, led by trans-Tasman VC firm Blackbird, will help the company expand its finance-automation software into New Zealand, Australia and the United States.
body: A Wellington-based artificial intelligence startup has raised $3.8 million in one of the larger seed funding rounds seen recently in New Zealand's technology sector. Sterling, which was founded just 10 months ago, develops software designed to automate routine finance and accounting work.

Chief executive and co-founder Nik Wakelin said Sterling was designed to act as an "autopilot" for finance teams rather than just another AI chatbot. "It sits in your finance team, in your inbox and all your systems, picks up things as they arrive and works out where everything goes and files it for you," he told RNZ. "The idea is by the time your finance team turns up in the morning and has their coffee, everything's done and prepped for them, ready to review and tick off."

Despite being only 10 months old, Sterling said it has been rolled out to users since March, and has already completed about 1200 hours of finance work for customers. Clients include honey exporter Manukora, early childhood software company Storypark and insurance broker Echelon.

The round was led by trans-Tasman venture capital firm Blackbird and included alumni from companies such as Xero, Vend, Pushpay and Trade Me, with the round also supported by Rowan Simpson, Eliot Crowther and other Kiwi founders-investors from those same companies. Co-founder Ludwig Wendzich, who worked at Vend, Lightspeed and Apple, said almost everyone at Sterling, including their investors, "cut their teeth" at companies such as Vend and Xero, adding: "We're the ones who learned how to build world-class software from New Zealand — now we're doing it again, for the people who keep every business running."

Wakelin is an engineer with two decades in startups, having co-founded time-tracking software MinuteDock and developer documentation tool Gelato.io before also holding a senior engineering role at Deliveroo. Wendzich spent close to a decade leading product and design at Vend and, following its acquisition, at Lightspeed, where he was Senior Director of Product Design.

Sterling says the fresh capital will help it expand in New Zealand, Australia and the United States. Wakelin said securing backing from Blackbird and well-known figures from New Zealand's technology sector would help accelerate the company's growth. "We really want to build the next generational technology company," he said.
stories.lens: There's no Hawke's Bay business behind this one, so the honest answer is that the region has no direct stake in Sterling's raise or its investors. Where it does matter is on the demand side: the Bay is thick with small and seasonal operations — orchards, wineries, contractors, tourism operators — that carry exactly the kind of repetitive invoicing, reconciliation and month-end workload Sterling says it can automate, and that's a genuine opportunity to cut back-office costs without adding headcount, if and when a Wellington-focused, enterprise-leaning startup like this actually turns its attention to smaller regional clients rather than the larger accounts it says it's chasing first. What the Bay could do is make sure its accountants, bookkeepers and business advisors — through bodies like the Hawke's Bay Chamber of Commerce or local accounting firms — keep an eye on tools like this as they mature, rather than assuming a Wellington-built product aimed at bigger customers will naturally suit a small orchard's books. What it should do is treat this as a skills issue as much as a tools issue: growers and small businesses eventually adopting AI finance automation will need staff who can supervise and sanity-check it, so regional training providers have a real opening to build basic AI-oversight literacy into bookkeeping and admin courses now, well ahead of the tools actually arriving on local doorsteps.

stories.headline: Havelock North's Margaret Thomas, 79, talks to Alexa before her feet hit the floor — and she's not alone
stories.brief: In her Havelock North retirement village townhouse, 79-year-old Margaret Thomas now runs her whole morning through an AI voice assistant, and she was one of 43 people aged 60 to 92 who attended Love Heart Social Learning's first Hawke's Bay AI workshop in June. The workshop's co-founder, educator Frances Valintine, says older Kiwis are far more switched-on to AI than they're given credit for — while also warning about deepfake risks.
body: Margaret Thomas wakes up about 8am each day, and before her feet even touch the floor, she starts talking to one of her closest daily companions. In her Havelock North retirement village townhouse, the 79-year-old has turned artificial intelligence into part of her daily routine. Alexa turns on the lights, boils the jug, starts the TV, plays music in the bedroom and adds items to her shopping list. "I just say, 'Alexa, cup of tea'," Margaret said.

Margaret was among 43 people, aged 60 to 92, who attended Love Heart Social Learning's first Hawke's Bay AI workshop in June, led by educator and Love Heart Social Learning co-founder Frances Valintine, who said learning it helped give seniors the confidence to feel connected to the world. She said older people were often underestimated. "I think other people make them feel left behind," Frances said. "Too many people put them in a box, saying they are of a certain age. My experience is that a lot of them are all over AI."

Frances said AI could help older people research holidays, create personalised cards, understand basic health information before seeing a doctor, or stay mentally engaged. But she also warned about the risks, saying AI "doesn't have a scamming ability as it's just generating a probability response" — while people are using AI to do a deepfake, to pretend to be someone.

For Margaret, technology does not replace people. "I still think there needs to be human interaction," she said. She is not interested in a future where robots replace nurses or carers entirely, although she can see the benefit of technology helping with physical tasks as people age.

Love Heart co-founder and managing director Fee Webby said the programme was designed for people aged over 60 who were still curious and wanted both learning and connection. "We need to make sure that we keep people cognitively engaged and we know the importance of ongoing learning for the brain to keep them stimulated," she said. "But also, more importantly, is that face-to-face connection."

Love Heart is a social enterprise founded by Hawke's Bay-based Fee Webby, who spent 10 years running private Auckland training establishment The Mind Lab, and Auckland tech educationalist and entrepreneur Frances Valintine CNZM. The programme began with a six-week Technological Impact course starting in Hawke's Bay on May 7, before expanding into Auckland with a six-week Society and Us course starting on June 4.

Fee, who lives in Hastings, said: "We're ageing differently and we expect more from the many decades we might live post-retirement." Love Heart launched in Hawke's Bay before popping up in other centres across Aotearoa, with the pair — who previously worked together building The Mind Lab — kicking off courses, activities and excursions across Hawke's Bay before expanding into Auckland. "Older people are healthier, more engaged and more intellectually curious than ever," Frances said.
stories.lens: This is a small story with an outsized point: the AI opportunity in Hawke's Bay isn't only about data centres and export manufacturing, it's also about digital confidence in a region with a large retired and semi-retired population, many living independently in retirement villages from Havelock North outward. Love Heart Social Learning has already shown there's real appetite here — 43 people turned up to a single June workshop, drawn from a Hawke's Bay-launched enterprise that has since expanded to Auckland — and that model could be scaled through retirement villages, libraries and community groups across Napier, Hastings and rural Hawke's Bay, pairing basic AI literacy with the scam and deepfake awareness Frances Valintine flagged as the real risk. Councils and community boards could back more sessions like this cheaply, aged-care providers could build simple voice-assistant setups into new tenancies as a selling point, and local retailers or health providers could use the same workshops to explain how AI tools might help with health information or daily tasks — all low-cost, high-trust moves that meet older residents where they already are, rather than chasing them into unfamiliar tech spaces. The flip side is real: as Margaret Thomas herself insists, no amount of AI literacy should be mistaken for a substitute for human contact and care, especially for a generation actively being targeted by AI-enabled scams.

stories.headline: Election looms, AI reshapes NZ jobs — but almost no party has a policy
stories.brief: With the 2026 general election approaching, The Spinoff reports that the Greens are so far the only party to have released any AI policy, calling for a one-year moratorium on new data centre consents, even as Prime Minister Christopher Luxon urges businesses to adopt AI tools and Finance Minister Nicola Willis banks on AI efficiency to help absorb 8,700 more public service job cuts.
body: New Zealand is heading into the 2026 general election with almost no political party having said what it would actually do about artificial intelligence. <cite index="13-8">To date, the only party to release any AI policy for the 2026 election is the Greens, which last week called for a one-year moratorium on new consents for data centres.</cite>

The policy vacuum comes despite AI already reshaping how the country's businesses and public service operate. <cite index="1-4">When prime minister Christopher Luxon addressed the crowd of the Rotorua business chamber last weekend in a now-infamous speech, he urged them to use Claude and Claude Code because "you have to disrupt yourself aggressively before you get disrupted by global events".</cite> <cite index="1-5">When finance minister Nicola Willis announced the government's intention to cut another 8,700 public service jobs, she was optimistic that artificial intelligence would help to make up for the reduced numbers with greater efficiency.</cite>

At the same time, the government is actively courting AI infrastructure investment. <cite index="1-6,1-7">Invest NZ, the government agency responsible for attracting foreign capital, is going all-in on AI-capable data centres as New Zealand's next big economic opportunity, actively recruiting support from New Zealand energy, utilities and construction companies and co-ordinating visits with international hyperscalers and hardware giants such as Nvidia and Microsoft.</cite> <cite index="13-7">In July 2025, the government announced a national strategy for artificial intelligence, though this was a "light-touch" approach which focused on encouraging small and medium businesses to adopt AI in their workflows and encouraged international investment.</cite>

Greens co-leader Chloe Swarbrick told The Spinoff <cite index="13-9">the party intended to release further AI policy but had prioritised the data centre issue because it was "physical infrastructure that has immediate impact on communities".</cite> <cite index="13-10">She described the moratorium as "breathing room" that would give the government time to develop new regulations for consenting.</cite> <cite index="13-11">"There very clearly is opportunity here but we need to have control over it and the impacts it will have economically, because right now the government seems to be taking a very agnostic approach," she said.</cite>

The piece frames the stakes as unusually high for New Zealand specifically. <cite index="13-3,13-4">Artificial intelligence is a technology with significant potential benefits and risks for every country, and New Zealand is likely to see more change than most — the country has significant industries in software and film production and the capacity to host a lot of data centres thanks to cool temperatures and capacity to increase renewable energy generation.</cite> Yet, <cite index="13-6">amidst all the hype of economic potential and fears of environmental, social and educational harm, there has so far been little actual policy proposed by any political parties about how exactly New Zealand is going to handle this enormous force that is invading our lives.</cite>
stories.lens: There's no direct Hawke's Bay angle in this story — it's about a gap in national election policy, not a local project or business — and it would be dishonest to force one. But the vacuum matters here precisely because it will be filled, or not, without local input unless the Bay makes noise now. Hastings and Napier district councils, the Hawke's Bay Regional Council and local chambers of commerce should be asking election candidates directly what they'd do on data centre siting, energy allocation and public-sector job losses, rather than waiting for policy to arrive fully formed from Wellington. Because central government is actively recruiting energy, utility and construction firms into the data-centre push, Bay businesses in those sectors have reason to find out whether that door is open to regional players, not just the big hyperscalers courted in Wellington and Auckland. For growers, orchardists and wineries, the more actionable takeaway is Luxon's blunt message to business: get using tools like Claude now, on rostering, spray-diary compliance, market reporting or admin, rather than waiting for a government AI strategy that so far amounts to little more than light-touch encouragement. And because Willis is explicitly counting on AI efficiency to cushion public-service job cuts, Bay residents in government-linked roles have a concrete reason to build AI fluency into their own skills now, rather than treating it as someone else's disruption.

stories.headline: Greens push for one-year pause on AI data centre consents as Southland's $3.5b Datagrid project fuels the fight
stories.brief: The Green Party has proposed a one-year national moratorium on consenting new AI data centres until proper regulations are in place, announcing the policy on Q+A after hundreds of people protested in Southland against a data centre that has already been consented there. The trigger is Singapore-based Datagrid's $3.5 billion hyperscale project at Makarewa, near Invercargill, which will need 280 MW of power and become the country's second-highest consumer of electricity. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has rejected the pause as "alarmist", while academics and Māori voices are asking whether such projects can ever secure genuine social licence.
body: Over the weekend the Green Party announced its proposal for a one-year national moratorium on the consenting of new artificial intelligence data centres until proper regulations have been set up, one of the sharper lines in the party's election manifesto released on Sunday. Co-leaders Chlöe Swarbrick and Marama Davidson framed the pause not as a ban on data storage or the internet, but as a chance to write proper rules before a wave of enormous facilities locks in decades of electricity demand, with the proposal covering the largest hyperscale developments and running only until national standards are in place.

At the centre of the debate is Singapore-based Datagrid, which was granted resource consent in March to build a $3.5 billion data centre at Makarewa, just north of Invercargill. The hyperscale project is set to be the second-highest consumer of electricity in the country, requiring 280 MW of power.

Swarbrick announced the moratorium policy on Q+A, after hundreds of people gathered in Southland to protest against the consented data centre, with councils accused of signing off on such projects behind closed doors. "Let's take a moment, let's have a common sense think about who they're actually benefitting, and whether New Zealanders want them in the first place," she said, adding that "this is not a ban on data infrastructure. It's a pause on the most resource-intensive developments while New Zealanders get a say on what conditions they should meet."

The policy sits inside a wider 43-page manifesto built around taxing wealth and lifting spending on public services, with Davidson saying "we will tax the super-rich and address corporate greed so that we can invest that back into the services that people rely on." On the data centre question specifically, Swarbrick argued "if we are going to let these things be built, we should at least understand who is benefitting and ensure we protect our natural resources and communities." Prime Minister Christopher Luxon rejected the call outright, describing the Greens as "alarmist" and saying the buildings were part of the plan for a bigger economy.

Supporters of such projects argue they will bring jobs and let New Zealand compete at the forefront of the AI industry, but critics have raised concerns about harm to the natural environment, the strain on energy and water resources, and the fact that projects have seemingly been approved with little public consultation. Critics have also argued the facilities will suck up power from the grid, push up electricity prices and create only a handful of jobs.

The debate has drawn in academic and Māori voices too. Dr Kerry McInerney, from the School of Computer Science at the University of Auckland, was interviewed on public perceptions of AI data centres in New Zealand, the concerns being raised, and whether such projects can secure a social licence — the idea that major infrastructure needs ongoing public confidence and acceptance, not simply regulatory approval, with trust depending on early engagement, transparency, accountability and evidence that communities will share in long-term benefits rather than just bear the costs. McInerney, who is of Ngāti Ruanui descent and researches AI ethics, governance, social justice and public trust, has noted that for Māori the debate carries added significance, with large-scale developments intersecting kaitiakitanga, environmental stewardship, Treaty relationships and questions of energy security, freshwater, whenua and data sovereignty.

The issue has become a live national political flashpoint rather than a niche environmental concern: NZ Herald political editor Thomas Coughlan discussed the Greens' one-year pause policy on Ryan Bridge TODAY this week. New Zealand's debate also echoes a similar one in Australia, where Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has announced large-scale data centres would face a legal obligation to underwrite new power supply, pay their full share of grid connection costs and cover any extra water infrastructure they require — legislation not expected to pass until early 2027.
stories.lens: Hawke's Bay has no hyperscale data centre bid on the table, and nothing in this story suggests one is coming, so the direct economic upside of a Datagrid-style project landing here isn't something to bank on. But the underlying fight — who gets access to scarce renewable electricity and water, and who gets a say before consent is granted — matters hugely to a region that already competes nationally for grid capacity and irrigation water for horticulture and wine. The Southland experience shows what happens when a consent this size is approved with, in protesters' view, too little warning: hundreds took to the streets months after the decision was made. If a national moratorium or new consenting rules for AI data centres come out of this debate, Hawke's Bay Regional Council and the Hastings and Napier councils should make sure the region's voice is in that policy conversation now, rather than finding out after the rules are set elsewhere. The Māori dimension of this debate — kaitiakitanga, Treaty relationships and data sovereignty — is also directly relevant here, given the Bay's iwi and hapū have long-standing stakes in freshwater and land decisions. The realistic play for the Bay isn't chasing a data centre of its own; it's making sure any national framework on AI infrastructure protects the water and power headroom local growers, wineries and manufacturers need, and pushing central government to treat genuine regional and iwi consultation as non-negotiable before, not after, consents are granted.

stories.headline: Biosecurity NZ trials AI to speed up the rules that keep pests out
stories.brief: Biosecurity New Zealand, part of the Ministry for Primary Industries, is running a four-month pilot using AI to help draft import health standards — the legal documents that govern which plants, animals and biological products can enter the country. Biosecurity Minister Andrew Hoggard announced the trial on 25 July.
body: Import health standards are the rulebook of New Zealand's border: the legal documents that decide which plants, animals and biological products can come in, and under what conditions. Biosecurity New Zealand has begun a four-month pilot using AI to help draft them, with Biosecurity Minister Andrew Hoggard announcing the trial on 25 July.

Hoggard framed it carefully as a productivity tool rather than a handover of judgement, saying it is about using smart tools to take on document-heavy work while key decisions remain with Biosecurity New Zealand's experts. The framework the standards sit within is more than 30 years old, and the document workload is significant.

The stakes behind the paperwork are large. New Zealand's food and fibre export revenue is forecast to reach $64.3 billion for the year ending 30 June 2026, and the Mycoplasma bovis eradication effort cost roughly $886 million over ten years — a reminder of what a biosecurity failure can cost the primary sector.
stories.lens: Hawke's Bay is one of the country's major horticulture and nursery regions, so the speed and quality of import health standards is not an abstract Wellington process — it shapes how quickly local growers can access new plant varieties, rootstock and genetics, and how well the border holds against the pests and diseases that would hit orchards and vineyards first. If AI can clear the document backlog without weakening the expert judgement at the core of these decisions, that is a direct benefit to the Bay. The region's growers, nurseries and industry bodies should make sure their needs are represented as the pilot is evaluated, so faster standards translate into real access to new material rather than just faster paperwork.

stories.headline: Kiwis use AI everywhere — and have mastered it almost nowhere
stories.brief: New Zealand now has its first national AI Strategy (“Investing with confidence”), betting on light-touch rules and fast adoption. Yet while 40–80% of organisations use AI in some form, just 2.7% of workers have it embedded in real workflows, and 79% of employers say they don’t know how to train staff — even as 90% expect AI-powered solutions running by 2028.
body: New Zealand now has its first national AI Strategy, “Investing with confidence,” released by MBIE. It is a deliberately light-touch framework that prioritises adoption and application over home-grown AI development, and leans on existing law rather than new AI-specific rules — betting that fast, safe uptake is the quickest route to lifting the country’s stubborn productivity.

The appetite is clearly there — depending on how usage is measured, somewhere between 40% and 80% of NZ organisations say they use AI in some form, according to the AI Forum’s review of adoption studies. But the usage is shallow. Analysis by consultancy Cairn finds only about 2.7% of the workforce qualify as genuine AI practitioners with the technology embedded in day-to-day workflows, and the typical organisation still rates itself at level 2 — “experimenting” — with a median maturity score of 2.4 out of 5.

The bottleneck is people, not tools. Around 79% of employers say they don’t know how to run an AI workforce-training programme, even as roughly 90% expect to be using AI-powered solutions by 2028. New Zealand also sits 37th on the global Government AI Readiness Index as of May 2026, with a stated ambition to climb into the top 30 by 2030 — the gap between enthusiasm and capability that is the whole ballgame.
stories.lens: The gap is the opportunity. If the national average organisation is still merely “experimenting,” a Hawke’s Bay firm that genuinely operationalises AI — not a chatbot bolted on the side, but AI wired into grading, forecasting, rostering or irrigation — leaps past city rivals still dabbling. The region’s advantage is that its problems are concrete: packhouses, wineries, coolstores, logistics and trades all have obvious, repetitive tasks where today’s tools already pay for themselves. The practical moves are unglamorous but decisive — pick one high-volume workflow per business and embed AI properly, lean on EIT and industry bodies to close the 79% training gap locally, and have councils and economic-development agencies treat AI capability as workforce infrastructure rather than a novelty. The honest caveat: a light-touch national strategy means none of this arrives on its own — the pull has to come from the Bay itself.

stories.headline: Microsoft doubles down on NZ AI skills as its cloud build-out ramps
stories.brief: Microsoft has doubled its New Zealand AI skilling target to 200,000 people by 2028 — up from 100,000 — and says it has already trained about 75,000, tying the push to its expanding cloud and data-centre footprint and the country’s AI capability gap.
body: Microsoft has sharply raised its ambitions for AI skills in New Zealand, announcing it will train 200,000 people by 2028 — double its earlier target of 100,000. The programme has already reached about 75,000 participants.

The push is tied directly to Microsoft’s hyperscale cloud and data-centre build-out in the country: as that infrastructure grows, it needs a local workforce able to deploy, secure and manage it. The training spans several strands, including Microsoft Elevate for Educators, Elevate for Changemakers, and a 10K Women programme.

The company frames it as an economic imperative. Its 2025 Work Trend Index found 59% of NZ business leaders believe productivity has to rise, and Microsoft estimates generative AI could add between NZ$76 billion and NZ$108 billion to the economy each year by 2038. “New Zealand is building strong momentum in AI adoption,” said Jane Livesey, president of Microsoft Australia and New Zealand. “However, now is not the time to take our foot off the accelerator.”
stories.lens: Skills are the bottleneck the adoption numbers keep hitting, and Microsoft’s training is largely free and delivered nationally — which makes it a lever the Bay can pull without funding it. The catch is that “national and online” is not the same as “local”: nobody in Wellington will route these places to Hawke’s Bay workers automatically. The concrete move is for Hi-Tech Hawke’s Bay, EIT and larger employers — the port, packhouses, councils — to actively channel staff into the Elevate and 10K Women programmes and build them into apprenticeship and retraining pathways. Done well, subsidised upskilling both lifts local workers and helps draw remote tech talent to the region; done passively, the training flows to the cities that ask for it first.

sectors.name: Solar & Energy
sectors.tag: The renewable boom — and why the sunny, storm-hit Bay has more at stake than most.

stories.headline: NZ's solar generation surges 66% in a year as renewables hit a record 47.7% of energy supply
stories.brief: MBIE's 2026 Energy in New Zealand report shows a 66% increase in solar generation over the past year to a new record, with several large utility-scale solar farms coming online, while the share of energy supply from renewable sources reached a new record high of 47.7% and 88.5% of electricity was generated from renewable sources in 2025.
body: The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment's 2026 Energy in New Zealand report shows that <cite index="1-1">solar generation rose 66% over the past year to a new record, with several large utility-scale solar farms coming online</cite>. <cite index="1-3">Geothermal generation also hit a record high in 2025.</cite>
<cite index="1-4">Solar generation is expected to continue increasing over the next few years, with many grid-connected solar plants currently under construction or in planning.</cite>

<cite index="1-5,1-6">While New Zealand's total energy supply decreased in 2025, mainly due to reduced coal and gas production, the share of energy supply from renewable sources reached a new record high of 47.7%, and renewables' contribution to overall energy supply has been growing since 2020.</cite> <cite index="1-7">In 2025, 88.5% of electricity was generated from renewable sources.</cite>

<cite index="12-9,12-10">Energy consumption from renewable sources increased to a record 32% of total consumption, reflecting both an increase in renewable supply and lower industrial demand for energy, which is mainly met from non-renewable sources.</cite> <cite index="3-4">Coal consumption fell to a record low in 2025, and natural gas consumption dropped to 2008 levels.</cite>
stories.lens: This is a national scorecard, but it lands on top of a real, already-underway Hawke's Bay project that fits the exact pattern MBIE describes — a utility-scale solar farm moving from planning into construction. Centralines and Lodestone Energy are building a $50 million solar farm on the Ruataniwha Plains near Ongaonga, comprising 49,000 solar panels on 14ha of a 34ha block that was previously dry stock farmland, expected to generate about 50GWh of renewable electricity a year — enough to power about 7000 homes — and to feed directly into the Centralines network, reducing the district's reliance on power carried in from elsewhere. Lodestone has described the region as one blessed with strong solar resources but historically hit hard by power prices, and Centralines expects the build to create up to 80 construction jobs, including around 30 skilled roles, with the farm due to be operating by late summer 2027. Central Hawke's Bay's mayor has framed new local generation as important for the district given rising electricity demand and the shift away from fossil fuels. The honest picture, though, is that this is still one project: the national data shows a wave of utility-scale solar reaching financial close and construction right now, and Hawke's Bay's stake in that wave is this single Ruataniwha Plains development rather than a fleet of completed farms. What the region can sensibly do is make sure this project actually gets built to schedule and delivers the promised local jobs and network benefits, and treat it as the template — proof that Hawke's Bay's sunshine and existing grid connections can attract serious investment — for any further utility-scale proposals that follow, rather than assuming national solar records automatically translate into local generation without projects like this one reaching completion.

stories.headline: Government moves to slash solar consent times from three months to six days
stories.brief: New Zealand's government has announced plans to simplify residential and small-to-medium scale solar approvals, cutting typical waiting times from three months to six days and costs from NZ$640 to NZ$200, according to Ministers Seymour and Brown. The move advances recommendations from a Ministry for Regulation sector review, which has also recommended legalising plug-in solar systems.
body: New Zealand's government has announced plans to simplify residential and small-to-medium scale solar approvals, pledging to cut waiting times from three months to six days and costs from NZ$640 to NZ$200, according to Ministers Seymour and Brown. The announcement advances the recommendations of the Ministry for Regulation's sector review report to simplify the installation of residential and small to medium scale solar panels, with the stated goal of making New Zealand the country where this process is simplest among developed economies.

The underlying review was ordered by the government, which described the existing approvals process as a "red tape nightmare" that can delay approvals for months, and set out to make New Zealand the "simplest developed country for solar deployment" by addressing barriers that currently require up to eight layers of sign-off and five separate site visits from four different entities before small-scale systems can be switched on. Regulation Minister David Seymour pointed to Victoria, Australia, as a potential model, where standard installations require just one layer of sign-off and can be approved within 24 hours, with installers managing the entire process and licensed electrical inspectors carrying out remote inspections using photographs unless non-compliance is identified. "During installation, the installer often cannot turn off or reconnect the fuse, update the meter, or carry out the required independent electrical inspection," Seymour said. "These tasks must be done by other entities, requiring additional site visits." Analysis by the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority cited in the review shows most New Zealand households could save more than NZ$1,000 annually on power bills by installing solar, with a typical small-to-medium system costing between NZ$8,500 and NZ$11,500 and paying for itself over about ten years. The push comes as New Zealand's distributed solar capacity increased 44% in 2025, with a record 258MW installed last year, according to data from Electricity Authority Te Mana Hiko.

As part of the same review, the Ministry for Regulation has also recommended legalising plug-in solar, alongside approving installations under 10kW by the next working day and allowing accredited installers to sign off installations under 100kW without an inspection. The report found that while demand for residential and business solar systems is increasing, prospective buyers face a time-consuming and frustrating customer journey due to the fragmented nature of existing regulations, and it suggests a series of changes to remove unnecessary barriers, reduce delays, speed up approvals and remove disproportionate requirements. "The report recommends legalizing plug-in solar because there was no good reason for preventing Kiwis using it," Seymour said. "Plug-in systems can be used by renters and people living in apartments who can't access traditional rooftop solar. If they're good enough for Germany and the UK, they're good enough for us." Energy Minister Simeon Brown welcomed the proposals, saying "New Zealanders want more control over their power bills and want to harness the power of the sun," and that the changes "will help give power back to the people by making solar uptake cheaper and faster."

On the numbers, once all the recommendations are implemented, the approval cost for a residential installation would fall from about NZ$640 over three months to NZ$200 over six days. For small-to-medium scale installations, such as panels installed on a farm milking shed, the cost would fall from up to NZ$11,000 over six months to NZ$1,300 over one month. The government also plans to shorten the processing times lines companies take to approve solar requests, with a standard residential request cut from ten working days to next-day processing. The Ministry estimates the recommendations could deliver net benefits of between NZ$28 million and NZ$50 million over ten years, through lower compliance costs, reduced delays and the use of plug-in solar.
stories.lens: This is a national process reform, not a local plant or investment, so there's no ribbon-cutting for Hawke's Bay here — but the practical effect lands directly on every Bay household, orchard, winery and small business weighing up rooftop or on-farm solar. If consent really does drop from three months and $640 to six days and $200, and lines companies start approving standard residential requests the next working day, that removes one of the biggest deterrents to going solar. The milking-shed example the Ministry itself uses — small-to-medium installations dropping from up to $11,000 and six months to $1,300 and one month — speaks directly to Hawke's Bay's orchards and wineries, many of which run exactly this kind of high daytime power draw for irrigation pumps, cool stores and processing sheds. The region could simply wait for the rules to filter through nationally; what it should do is get ahead of them. Local councils have limited ability to change electricity-network or building-consent rules themselves, since those sit with central government and lines companies, but they can make sure their own permitted-activity and building-consent processes aren't adding extra friction on top of the national reform once it lands. Local electricians and solar installers should also prepare for a possible jump in enquiries once the cost and wait-time barriers fall — and if plug-in solar is eventually legalised, that opens a cheaper entry point for the Bay's renters and apartment dwellers who currently have no realistic access to solar at all.

stories.headline: Hawke's Bay's first utility-scale solar farm breaks ground in Central Hawke's Bay
stories.brief: Construction has begun on the region's first utility-scale solar farm, a 31.5 MWp project on the Ruataniwha Plains in Central Hawke's Bay, built by Lodestone Energy in a joint venture with consumer-owned local lines company Centralines. The roughly NZ$50 million, 34-hectare development will use 49,168 panels and generate about 50 GWh a year — enough for around 7,000 households.
body: A ceremonial groundbreaking on the Ruataniwha Plains has started work on what will be Hawke's Bay's first utility-scale solar farm. The project pairs national developer Lodestone Energy with Centralines, the consumer-owned lines company for Central Hawke's Bay, and the power it produces will feed directly into the Centralines network — local generation for local lines.

The numbers are substantial for the region: 31.5 MWp of capacity across about 34 hectares, 49,168 panels, and an expected output of roughly 50 GWh a year, enough to cover around 7,000 households. ASB reached financial close on the roughly NZ$50 million project on 10 July 2026, and it is expected to be operational by autumn 2027.

It is also an agrivoltaic build: sheep grazing will continue beneath the panels on land previously used for dry-stock grazing, so the site keeps earning as farmland while it generates electricity. Centralines chair Fenton Wilson called it a long-term investment in the region's future, and Lodestone managing director Gary Holden framed it as adding renewable capacity while delivering benefits closer to home.
stories.lens: This is exactly the kind of infrastructure a region exposed to cyclones, drought and volatile power prices should want: renewable generation owned partly by the community lines company and feeding the local network. The template it sets — agrivoltaics that keep grazing income while producing power — is well suited to Hawke's Bay's marginal and dry-stock land, and the Bay could deliberately pursue more of it: growers and packhouses partnering on generation to cut and stabilise their own energy costs, councils smoothing consenting for well-sited projects, and Centralines building on this first project to improve local resilience after weather events. The move from importing power to generating it locally is a concrete regional-resilience win, and the region should treat this as the first of many rather than a novelty.

stories.headline: NZ quietly ticks past 1 gigawatt of local solar — and businesses now out-panel homes
stories.brief: New figures reported by NewsWire, drawn from Electricity Authority data, show New Zealand's local networks crossed 1,020 megawatts of installed solar as of 30 June 2026, spread across 88,412 connections — a milestone that arrived unannounced sometime in May. Nationally 80,463 homes now have solar, about one in 25 residential connections, up from one in 160 a decade ago, and around 22% of solar connections now have a battery attached. Businesses now hold more solar capacity — 565MW — than every home in the country combined, on 456MW.
body: New Zealand has passed a quiet but significant energy threshold: total solar capacity connected to local lines networks has topped one gigawatt. According to figures reported by NewsWire from newly updated Electricity Authority data, the country slipped past the mark sometime in May 2026, with no ribbon-cutting and no press release to mark it.

The figures, which NewsWire drew from the Electricity Authority's distributed-generation series to 30 June 2026, show 1,020 megawatts of solar installed across 88,412 connections nationwide, and confirm that businesses now hold more of that capacity — 565 megawatts across 7,949 business connections — than every home in the country combined, on 456 megawatts. The one-gigawatt total is more nameplate capacity than Manapouri, the country's largest hydro station at 850 megawatts — though a megawatt of solar produces far less energy over a year than a megawatt of hydro, so the milestone is more about the sheer volume of hardware installed than a shift in the generation mix.

Regionally, the uptake picture is uneven. Auckland has more solar connections than anywhere else — 14,877 of them — yet it sits near the bottom of the table on uptake, with panels on just 2.4 percent of homes, ranking 14th of 16 regions. By contrast, the top of the South Island owns the leaderboard: Tasman leads the country at 9.1 percent, with Nelson on 7.5 percent and Marlborough on 7.0 percent — against Auckland's 2.4 percent — while the wet, sparsely populated West Coast sits last at 1.9 percent. Nationally, 80,463 homes have solar, about one in every 25 residential connections, up from about one home in 160 a decade ago.

Batteries are increasingly following the panels onto rooftops. At least 19,579 solar connections — around 22 percent — are recorded as having a battery attached, and because retrofits don't always show up in network records, the real figure is likely higher. Roughly 369 megawatts of solar was added in the year to June 2026, and at that pace NewsWire suggests the second gigawatt could arrive around 2029 — though the trajectory has been accelerating.
stories.lens: For Hawke's Bay the timing is pointed: the region is only now gaining its first utility-scale solar farm. Lodestone Energy and lines company Centralines have broken ground on a 31.5 MW, roughly $50 million agrivoltaic plant on the Ruataniwha Plains in Central Hawke's Bay — around 49,000 panels expected to generate about 50 GWh a year, with grazing continuing beneath them — and commercial operation is due in late summer 2027. Developers describe it as filling a longstanding gap in the Bay's energy mix, and it is unlikely to be the last: further projects are proposed nearby, including a Helios Energy farm at Ongaonga and larger developments again on the regional boundary. The clearest lesson from the national figures is that sunshine alone does not drive uptake — sunny Auckland ranks near the bottom — so the Bay's real advantage is one it has to choose: councils resourcing fast, predictable consenting for rooftop and farm-scale arrays; growers, packhouses and coolstores pairing panels with batteries to cut daytime power costs and firm supply after Gabrielle-era outages; and local installers and electricians building the workforce so the jobs and network-resilience benefits of this gigawatt milestone land in the region rather than pass it by.

stories.headline: NZ's biggest solar farm just switched on — and it won't hold the title for long
stories.brief: The 150 MW Tauhei Solar Farm near Hamilton energised on 15 July 2026 — nearly 330,000 panels generating an estimated 280 GWh a year, enough to power about 35,000 homes, with Meridian buying 100% of output for a decade. It dwarfs the previous 47 MW record and leads a wave of grid-scale projects racing to connect as costs fall.
body: New Zealand's largest solar farm has come online. The 150 MW Tauhei Solar Farm, on a 182-hectare site near Hamilton in the Waikato, was energised on 15 July 2026, its almost 330,000 panels able to generate an estimated 280 GWh of electricity a year — enough to power roughly 35,000 homes.

Built by UK-headquartered Harmony Energy with backing from infrastructure investor Igneo Infrastructure Partners, the farm has a deal with Meridian Energy to buy 100% of its output for the first 10 years of operation — the kind of long-term power-purchase agreement that makes utility-scale solar bankable. It dwarfs the country's previous record-holder, the 47 MW Lauriston Solar Farm developed by Genesis and FRV near Christchurch in Canterbury.

Tauhei is the biggest of a wave. Grid-connected solar has moved from a rounding error to a fast-growing slice of New Zealand's generation as panel costs fall and consenting speeds up. The Electricity Authority reports that 247 MW of grid-connected solar has been installed since 2023, with solar setting a new half-hourly record of 210 MW on 30 January 2026 and a pipeline of large projects — some 783 MW expected in 2026/27 — racing to connect over the next few years.
stories.lens: Hawke's Bay is one of the country's sunniest regions, which makes grid-scale solar a natural fit — and, with Lodestone and Centralines' Ruataniwha Plains farm now under construction, no longer hypothetical. For energy-hungry packhouses and coolstores, cheaper daytime power is the direct prize; for landowners, a generation lease is new revenue from the same paddock; and after Cyclone Gabrielle severed power to much of the region, local generation paired with batteries is a tangible resilience play. The concrete move for the Bay is to treat Tauhei as a proof point and get the enabling work done early: councils resourcing fast, predictable consenting, lines companies planning grid capacity for connection, and growers and cooperatives lining up power-purchase deals so the next wave of projects chooses Hawke's Bay rather than passing it by.

stories.headline: Sheep graze under the panels — and 32 farms trial solar and batteries
stories.brief: New Zealand's EECA has selected 32 farms for a solar-and-battery trial — its 'Solar on Farms' programme — collectively installing about 3,616 kW of generation across dairy, sheep, beef, horticulture, poultry, nursery and wine operations. Separately, agrivoltaic sites like the Rangitaiki solar farm in the Bay of Plenty already run sheep beneath raised panels, generating power and farming the same land.
body: New Zealand is testing, on two fronts, whether farms can generate power without giving up productive land. The government's Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority (EECA) has selected 32 farms for a solar-and-battery trial under its 'Solar on Farms' programme, with the properties collectively installing about 3,616 kW of solar — systems ranging from 30 kW to well over 150 kW, plus four battery-only sites — across dairy, sheep, beef, horticulture, poultry, nursery and wine operations. One participant, the Balle Bros Group, has paired a 216 kW array on a packhouse roof with a 116 kWh battery. In return for partial funding, the farms will share performance data and host demonstration events to encourage wider uptake.

The more eye-catching idea is agrivoltaics — farming directly beneath the panels. At Lodestone Energy's 32 MW Rangitaiki solar farm near Edgecumbe in the Bay of Plenty, nearly 60,000 bi-facial panels sit on trackers mounted high enough for sheep to graze and move freely underneath, with the operator reporting that roughly 80 percent of grass productivity is retained while the panels provide shade. Lodestone is also trialling strawberry cultivation between the rows, treating the site as a prototype for pairing generation with farming rather than displacing it.

The appeal is dual use of the same hectares: a generation lease or on-farm power on top of ordinary farm returns, sheep doubling as low-cost vegetation control, shade and shelter for stock, and — where batteries are added, as in the EECA trial — a measure of on-farm energy security. For a country wrestling with how to decarbonise without paving over productive land, 'solar and food' is a far easier proposition than 'solar or food.'
stories.lens: This is the solar story that fits a farming region best. Hawke's Bay's sheep-and-beef blocks, orchards and vineyards could earn a second income from generation on land they already farm, with raised panels adding shade and shelter for stock and batteries firming supply on remote blocks. The practical steps are unglamorous but decisive: growers and station owners running the numbers on a generation lease versus rooftop-and-battery ownership; industry bodies and EECA bringing a Bay farm into the next demonstration round so the data is local, not just Bay-of-Plenty; and lines companies signalling where on the network farm-scale solar can connect. Done well, solar vs food becomes solar and food — extra revenue and resilience without taking a hectare out of production.

sectors.name: Connectivity
sectors.tag: Satellites and rural broadband lifting the ceiling on what the back-country can do.

stories.headline: Direct-to-Cell Satellites Are Closing New Zealand's Rural Mobile Gap, Gartner Analyst Says
stories.brief: Space-based cellular networks are reshaping Aotearoa's mobile market, according to Gartner analyst Khurram Shahzad, interviewed by journalist Bill Bennett. Mobile networks cover roughly 98 percent of New Zealand's population but only about 50 percent of the landmass, and Shahzad says direct-to-device satellite technology exists precisely because regulators expect telcos to deliver universal coverage that isn't otherwise economical.
body: Space-based cellular networks are reshaping Aotearoa's market, Bill Bennett reports after interviewing Khurram Shahzad, Senior Director Analyst at Gartner, about the forces driving New Zealand telcos toward direct-to-device (D2D) satellite technology.

The scale of the coverage problem is stark: mobile networks reach roughly 98 percent of New Zealand's population but only about 50 percent of the landmass. Unlike Australia's more metro-centric population, New Zealand has far more people living outside major urban centres, which Shahzad says partly explains why low-Earth orbit satellites have seen record per-capita uptake here.

For mobile operators, D2D solves a specific problem. As Shahzad puts it, "The biggest pain point of telcos is that they had the expectation by the regulators that they will provide universal coverage. This is just not economical." By partnering with Starlink, he says, that burden is lifted from telcos, since they no longer have to deploy towers in rural areas to meet that expectation.
stories.lens: Hawke's Bay is a near-perfect illustration of the gap Shahzad describes: inland ranges, hill country farms and remote parts of Wairoa and Central Hawke's Bay sit well outside the roughly 50 percent of the national landmass that conventional mobile towers reach, even though population coverage nationally looks high. That mismatch between population-coverage statistics and landmass-coverage reality is exactly why direct-to-cell satellite technology matters here more than in a metro-heavy market. The honest takeaway for the region is that this is a genuine structural fix, not a marketing gimmick: if telcos are turning to satellite partnerships because blanket tower coverage was never going to be economical in low-density, hilly terrain, then Hawke's Bay's isolated farms, orchards and lifestyle blocks are precisely the customers this technology is built for. Local councils and rural business groups should treat improving D2D handset compatibility and coverage advice as a practical advocacy target with telcos, rather than waiting for fibre or new towers that may never be commercially justified for the most remote parts of the region.

stories.headline: NZ internet providers call for a market study into Starlink's rural grip
stories.brief: The Internet Service Providers Association of New Zealand (Ispanz) has written an open letter to Telecommunications Commissioner Tristan Gilbertson asking for a formal market study under Part 3A of the Commerce Act into Starlink's impact, noting Starlink is now the largest rural internet provider in New Zealand.
body: New Zealand's internet providers are asking the regulator to take a hard look at Starlink. In an open letter to Telecommunications Commissioner Tristan Gilbertson, industry body Ispanz has requested a formal market study under Part 3A of the Commerce Act, arguing that Starlink has become the largest rural internet provider in the country and that the rural connectivity market is tilting fast.

Ispanz frames the concern as national resilience rather than simple competition. It warns that if the local industry is hollowed out, local engineering expertise, field workforces and operational knowledge could all disappear — capabilities that matter when networks need to be fixed after a storm.

Its proposed remedy is wholesale access: requiring Starlink and other low-earth-orbit providers to offer wholesale services so New Zealand firms can build value on top — installation, managed networking, WiFi, cybersecurity and farm-connectivity services — rather than being reduced to bystanders.
stories.lens: Rural Hawke's Bay has a direct stake in how this plays out. Satellite broadband has been transformative for farms, orchards and remote households that copper and fixed wireless never served well, and Cyclone Gabrielle showed how much resilient connectivity matters here. But if the local installer and engineering base that keeps rural networks running is squeezed out, the Bay loses the very people who show up when connections fail. The regional interest is a market that keeps satellite's reach while preserving local skills and jobs — so local ISPs, installers and farm-connectivity specialists should be part of this conversation, and rural communities, marae and growers should push for resilient options that do not depend on a single overseas provider.

stories.headline: Your phone now texts via satellite across the 40% of NZ that had no coverage
stories.brief: One NZ’s satellite service — using Starlink’s direct-to-mobile tech — now reaches ordinary phones across roughly 40% of NZ’s landmass that had no cell coverage, starting with texting (free on eligible plans) and expanding to data, apps and calling.
body: Large parts of rural New Zealand have never had mobile coverage. That is changing: One NZ’s satellite service, built on Starlink’s direct-to-mobile technology, now reaches ordinary smartphones across roughly 40% of the country’s landmass that sits beyond any cell tower’s range — no satellite dish or dedicated hardware, just a supported handset. One NZ says it was the first telecommunications company in the world to launch a nationwide Starlink Direct to Mobile service.

It launched with text messaging — free on eligible Pay Monthly and business plans — in December 2024, and in its first year carried around 7 million messages to more than 700,000 customers. From February 2026 the service began expanding beyond texting to satellite data, apps such as Google Maps and AllTrails, and WhatsApp voice calling, and rival Spark launched its own competing satellite text service in April 2026.

For anyone who tramps, farms or lives beyond the towers, it turns a dead phone into a working one — able to send a text from a back paddock or a remote hut. It is the connectivity floor rising for the roughly 40% of the map conventional networks never reached.
stories.lens: Connectivity has always been the low ceiling on rural technology, and this lifts it almost automatically — any Hawke’s Bay farmer, forestry crew or back-country worker with a supported phone gets coverage across country that never had it, with nothing the region itself has to build or fund. The honest point is that this is a national telco capability the Bay simply inherits rather than something it has to win. Where the region can act is on top of it: emergency managers should fold satellite messaging into civil-defence planning after Cyclone Gabrielle exposed how fragile rural comms are; farm, orchard and forestry employers can lean on it for lone-worker safety in the hills; and agritech that depends on a signal — smart collars, remote sensors, precision irrigation — becomes deployable across Wairoa, the coast and the Central Hawke’s Bay hill blocks where coverage was never a given.

stories.headline: How Starlink quietly became rural New Zealand’s default internet
stories.brief: Beyond phones, Starlink has become rural New Zealand’s default broadband — around 85,000 connections (roughly 72,000 rural) and about a 27% rural market share, making it the country’s largest rural internet provider. A Federated Farmers survey put satellite use on farms at 36%.
body: Away from the phone network, Starlink has quietly become rural New Zealand’s default internet. In the year to June 2025, SpaceX’s satellite service grew from about 58,000 connections to 85,000 — roughly 72,000 of them rural and 13,000 urban — making it the country’s largest rural internet provider on around a 27% share, as its qualifying NZ revenue jumped 38% to about $101 million.

The shift shows in the paddock data. A Federated Farmers survey found satellite internet use on farms rising to 36%, while traditional wireless broadband slipped to 44% — a clear move toward satellite, even though fixed wireless narrowly remains the most common rural connection. New Zealand now has the highest per-capita satellite broadband adoption in the OECD. Plans run roughly $85 to $170 a month after a mid-2026 price rise, with hardware around $799 upfront.

The upside is fibre-like speed in places fixed networks abandoned — video calls, live data from the woolshed, streaming in the evening. The catch is concentration: an independent report for the Commerce Commission by Richard Feasey warned of a “material risk” that Starlink could become the dominant or monopoly supplier in rural areas, which would make any future intervention difficult, and local wireless providers are already feeling the squeeze — the Bay of Plenty operator Evolution Networks has gone into liquidation.
stories.lens: For the Bay’s back-country growers and coastal stations, reliable broadband is the difference between “someday” and “deployable” for data-driven farming, and it makes rural remote work, telehealth and online education genuinely workable in places fixed lines never reached. That reframes what regional investment should target: connectivity is now largely a solved problem in the hills, so councils and economic-development agencies can pivot to what runs on top of it — agritech, remote tech jobs, rural upskilling. The honest caveat is concentration risk. With the Commerce Commission already flagging Starlink’s monopoly potential and local wireless operators folding, the Bay would be unwise to let a single offshore provider become the only pipe into the back-country; keeping local wireless firms and fibre extension alive is a resilience play worth backing.
