stories.headline: Meet the 79-year-old Havelock North woman who's made AI part of her daily routine
stories.brief: Margaret Thomas, 79, has turned artificial intelligence into part of daily life in her Havelock North retirement village townhouse, using Alexa to run her mornings, evenings and even her travel journalling. She was one of 43 people aged 60 to 92 who attended Love Heart Social Learning's first Hawke's Bay AI workshop in June, co-founded by educator Frances Valintine and Fee Webby.
body: Margaret Thomas wakes up about 8am each day, and before her feet even touch the floor, she starts talking to one of her closest daily companions. In her Havelock North retirement village townhouse, the 79-year-old has turned artificial intelligence into part of her daily routine. Alexa turns on the lights, boils the jug, starts the TV, plays music in the bedroom and adds items to her shopping list. When she wants a cup of tea, she does not walk first to the kitchen — she waits for the kettle to boil after asking Alexa to switch it on. "I just say, 'Alexa, cup of tea'," Margaret said. The jug starts boiling.

Margaret Thomas keeps an Alexa device beside her bed, using it to start and end each day with voice commands. When she is ready to sleep, she doesn't reach for a switch — she simply calls out and the system turns off the TV and lights. She has also used technology to record her travels, creating a travel journal with the Find Penguins app.

For all her comfort with the devices, Margaret is clear about where she draws the line. "For Margaret, technology does not replace people," and she said: "I still think there needs to be human interaction." She is not interested in a future where robots replace nurses or carers entirely, although she can see the benefit of technology helping with physical tasks as people age.

For some people, artificial intelligence is still something distant, strange or even frightening — but Margaret is far from the only older Hawke's Bay resident embracing new technology. She was among 43 people, aged 60 to 92, who attended Love Heart Social Learning's first Hawke's Bay AI workshop in June, led by educator and Love Heart Social Learning co-founder Frances Valintine, who said learning it helped give seniors the confidence to feel connected to the world.

Valintine said older people were often underestimated. "I think other people make them feel left behind," she said. "Too many people put them in a box, saying they are of a certain age. My experience is that a lot of them are all over AI." She said AI could help older people research holidays, create personalised cards, understand basic health information before seeing a doctor, or stay mentally engaged.

Love Heart co-founder and managing director Fee Webby said the programme was designed for people aged over 60 who were still curious and wanted both learning and connection. "We need to make sure that we keep people cognitively engaged and we know the importance of ongoing learning for the brain to keep them stimulated," she said. "But also, more importantly, is that face-to-face connection."

The story of Margaret and her Alexa routine is part of a wider examination by Hawke's Bay Today reporter Rafaella Melo, in her 'The Years Ahead' series, of the role technology is playing in transforming the lives of Hawke's Bay seniors.
stories.lens: What's striking here isn't the gadgetry — it's the balance. Margaret Thomas has let Alexa run her lights, kettle and bedtime, yet she and Love Heart's own organisers are just as insistent that none of it should replace a person: she doesn't want robots replacing nurses, and Fee Webby says the real point of these sessions is face-to-face connection as much as digital skill. That's a useful corrective for any Hawke's Bay push on seniors and technology — the goal shouldn't be to digitise care but to use tools like voice assistants to support independence while keeping human contact central. Forty-three people turning out for one workshop, spanning ages 60 to 92, is a small but real data point that appetite exists locally; it doesn't prove a region-wide trend, but it does suggest more structured, social AI-literacy sessions — modelled on what Valintine and Webby are already running in Hawke's Bay — could find an audience if offered through retirement villages and community groups. The honest limit is that this is one cohort in one workshop, not evidence of scale, and any expansion should follow the same principle its founders emphasise: technology as a companion to connection, not a substitute for it.

stories.headline: Hastings IT firm grows on a 13-year EIT graduate pipeline
stories.brief: A local feature highlights the partnership — running since 2013 — between the Eastern Institute of Technology and Hastings IT firm Hawke's Bay Technologies, which has grown from 10 to 32 employees while recruiting EIT graduates across engineering, finance and technical support.
body: Not every Hawke's Bay tech story is a robot or a rocket; some are about the quieter machinery of growing a local firm. Hastings IT company Hawke's Bay Technologies has expanded from 10 to 32 employees, and it credits a 13-year partnership with the Eastern Institute of Technology, running since 2013, as a steady source of the people it needs.

The firm recruits EIT graduates across engineering, finance and technical support. Managing director Duncan Wallace says the graduates arrive job-ready and get up and running from day one, while service desk engineer Zachariah Hull points to EIT's hands-on training as the reason.

It is a small case study in something the region needs more of: a local tertiary institution feeding trained people straight into local tech employers, so that graduates build their careers in Hawke's Bay rather than leaving for the main centres.
stories.lens: The single biggest constraint on a regional tech economy is people, and this is what the answer looks like in practice — a local training pipeline feeding local employers, keeping graduates in the Bay. The region should protect and grow it: back EIT's technology and engineering programmes, encourage more Hawke's Bay firms to build formal graduate pathways the way Hawke's Bay Technologies has, and treat graduate retention as an economic-development metric that matters. Every marquee story on this site — Hawk Technology's robots, Rocket Lab at Māhia, the new solar farm — ultimately needs a deep local skills base to draw on, and that base is built one graduate pipeline at a time.

stories.headline: Hawke's Bay drone firm lands NZ-first certification — and a $60m Australasia distribution deal
stories.brief: Hawke's Bay-based Aerospread Technologies has a New Zealand first: its xFold H500 heavy-lift drone (200kg payload) is the first aircraft of its class to win full CAA Part 102 certification for unrestricted agricultural operations in New Zealand. The milestone was revealed alongside a distribution deal in which US-based Powerus, via subsidiary Kaizen Aerospace, named the Napier company its exclusive agent for the xFold platform across Australia, New Zealand and the South Pacific — with performance-based targets of about $60 million in product revenue over five years (targets, not binding orders).
body: A locally built aviation story just went global. Aerospread Technologies, which operates from a purpose-built facility in Hawke's Bay, has notched a genuine New Zealand first: its xFold H500, a 200kg-payload heavy-lift drone, is now the first aircraft of its class to receive full CAA Part 102 certification for unrestricted agricultural operations in New Zealand — clearing a regulatory bar that has held back large autonomous ag-aircraft.

The certification was revealed alongside a major commercial deal. US-based Autonomous Power Corporation, trading as Powerus and based in West Palm Beach, Florida, announced that its wholly owned subsidiary Kaizen Aerospace had launched a dedicated agriculture division and appointed Aerospread Technologies as its exclusive agent for xFold sales and distribution across the Australia and New Zealand markets and the wider South Pacific. Based on Aerospread's projected volumes, the sales targets represent roughly $60 million in potential product revenue over the first five years — though the companies stress these are performance objectives, not binding purchase commitments.

The same announcement revealed a parallel US arrangement. Benton, Kentucky-based Sprig Aerospace became an authorised distributor and marketing partner that will standardise its commercial spraying and aerial-application fleet on Powerus xFold aircraft, and the FAA issued Sprig a Special Airworthiness Certificate (Experimental Category), plus a Certificate of Waiver of Authorization, for the larger xFold Dragon H1000 for research and development. That places the Hawke's Bay operation at the centre of an international rollout of heavy-lift agricultural drone technology, rather than a bit-part local supply arrangement.

Aerospread, founded in 2017 by veteran agricultural pilot Bruce Peterson, has grown from a topdressing operator into a manufacturer and technology developer in its own right, running its aerial services under the Aerotech UAV brand while Aerospread Technologies Ltd drives the innovation, manufacturing and certification work behind it.
stories.lens: This is a rare case of a Hawke's Bay-headquartered company setting the pace rather than adopting someone else's technology — the CAA Part 102 milestone was won on home soil, at a Hawke's Bay facility, before the company was handed distribution rights spanning Australia, New Zealand and the South Pacific. To build on it, the region could keep the high-value engineering, flight-testing and regulatory work anchored locally rather than letting it drift offshore as the deal scales; grow a supply chain of drone technicians, remote pilots and maintenance crews through local training providers and the Hi-Tech Hawke's Bay network; and get growers trialling heavy-lift autonomous spraying and spreading on the orchard, vineyard and steep forestry blocks where labour is scarcest. Positioning the Bay as New Zealand's proving ground for large agricultural UAVs — with councils and investors backing the certification and testing capability that already sits here — is how a single world-class win becomes a durable local cluster.

stories.headline: The Bay quietly built a food-innovation campus — and it's filling up
stories.brief: Foodeast Haumako, a purpose-built food, beverage and agritech innovation centre at Tomoana, Hastings, offers 600m² production and warehouse bays, office tenancies, meeting and conference space, and a startup-support model — and already houses businesses including Mara Bio, AsureQuality and the New Zealand Food Innovation Network.
body: Hawke's Bay has quietly built itself a home for food innovation. Foodeast Haumako, a purpose-built food, beverage and agritech innovation centre at 4 Hanui Road, Tomoana, Hastings, sets out to be "New Zealand's leading catalyser of commercially successful food innovation" — offering the physical and commercial scaffolding local makers have long lacked.

The site pairs light-filled office tenancies of varying sizes with four 600-square-metre production and warehouse bays, two tech-forward meeting rooms, a boardroom and a dedicated conference space, plus an action-oriented startup-support model. It already houses businesses including Mara Bio, AsureQuality, the New Zealand Food Innovation Network and the Bioresource Processing Alliance, and runs a "Sustainable is Attainable" programme aimed at developing viable alternatives for the waste and by-products generated during food processing and manufacturing.

For a region that grows an enormous volume of raw product but has often watched the value-add happen elsewhere, a place to prototype, scale and commercialise without leaving the Bay is exactly the missing piece.
stories.lens: This is the physical backbone the region's foodtech ambitions have lacked — somewhere Bay growers and makers can prototype, scale and commercialise without shipping the value-add out of the province. To push the momentum further, the priority is simple: fill the bays with local ventures moving beyond raw commodity, and wire the campus tightly into the region's growers and processors so more of the margin is captured here. The "Sustainable is Attainable" stream is a concrete lever — turning packhouse and processing waste into saleable products — while councils and investors could back tenancy incentives and shared-equipment access so early-stage food ventures can reach commercial scale without leaving Hawke's Bay.

stories.headline: Napier Port bets up to $25m on self-driving trucks — a first for NZ ports
stories.brief: Napier Port plans a fleet of about a dozen battery-electric autonomous trucks to move containers around its terminal — an investment estimated at $20–25 million, a first for a New Zealand port. The Maritime Union has warned the automation is "a threat to jobs, safety, and productivity."
body: Napier Port is preparing to become the first port in New Zealand to run a fleet of autonomous trucks. The plan, estimated at $20–25 million including a battery-swap station, would put about a dozen battery-electric self-driving vehicles to work loading and shifting containers within the container terminal. The first truck was due to arrive from China in the first half of 2026, with the rest of the fleet later in the year. The port frames it as a productivity and safety upgrade — pairing the fleet with a new one-way traffic system it says will cut the major risk of vehicle collision — for the Bay's main export gateway, a company majority-owned by the Hawke's Bay Regional Council.

It hasn't landed without friction. The Maritime Union of New Zealand pushed back on 26 September 2025, with national secretary Carl Findlay calling the move "a threat to jobs, safety, and productivity across the sector" and pointing to Ports of Auckland's abandoned automated straddle-carrier programme in 2022 as a cautionary tale. The port has acknowledged the shift will bring a small number of redundancies among heavy-plant operators, while noting new roles are emerging — 11 staff are already completing an electric-vehicle engineering certificate.

That tension is the story. Napier Port is the route to market for the region's apples, wine, timber and squash, so anything that makes it faster and more competitive matters — but so do the port jobs that come with it. It is precisely the kind of shift that reads differently through a Hawke's Bay lens than a national one.
stories.lens: The Bay's export gateway going automated is a genuinely two-sided local story — competitiveness on one hand, port jobs on the other. Because Napier Port is majority-owned by the Hawke's Bay Regional Council, the region has real leverage to shape a just transition: redeploy and retrain displaced heavy-plant operators into the EV-engineering, maintenance and control-room roles the new fleet creates (the 11 staff already on an EV certificate are the model), and make sure the productivity gains flow back into the regional economy rather than out of it. Getting the union, the port and the council around the same table early is how the Bay captures the efficiency without hollowing out the workforce that depends on it.

stories.headline: Hi-tech is quietly blossoming across Hawke's Bay
stories.brief: Beyond the headline names, a growing base of tech firms is taking root across the Bay — just under 500 firms in high-tech manufacturing and ICT, employing more than 1,500 people, with the Hi-Tech Hawke's Bay network alone counting around 240 members.
body: Beneath the headline names, Hawke's Bay has grown a surprisingly deep tech base. The region is now home to just under 500 firms across high-tech manufacturing and ICT, employing more than 1,500 people, and the Hi-Tech Hawke's Bay network alone counts around 240 members.

The roster runs well beyond Rocket Lab: Fingermark, software firms like Re-leased and Ask Your Team, StockX, agri-data players HortPlus and MyEnviro, and automation specialists such as MHM Automation, CR Automation and RBE Hortworx — alongside big local names Pan Pac and Napier Port. Xero founder Rod Drury keeps an office in the Ahuriri Tech Collective, a shared workspace whose tenants include NOW, WebFox and Re-leased and which has become a hub for the scene.

Under it sits a talent pipeline: the iwi-led Puhoro STEM programme, which began delivering in Hawke's Bay in 2021 and has supported dozens of rangatahi into tech skills, and a Rocket Lab education centre coming to Wairoa backed by a $6 million Provincial Growth Fund grant. "It's hard to define tech as one thing," says Hi-Tech Hawke's Bay chair Dave France. "We're moving fast as a region and even the most traditional industries are using or developing digital capabilities in some form or another." Surfacing and connecting these firms is exactly how a scattered scene becomes an ecosystem.
stories.lens: This is the grassroots the region's tech-growth story is built on — a scene, not yet fully an ecosystem. The concrete moves that would push the momentum further are unglamorous but real: keep surfacing and connecting the firms so they can share talent, tooling and customers rather than compete blind; feed the talent pipeline by scaling Puhoro STEM and the Wairoa education centre so young Māori and rural students have a genuine local path into tech; and lean on models like the Ahuriri Tech Collective — plus remote-work-friendly lifestyle — to keep graduates in the Bay and draw others back. A region that deliberately stitches 500 scattered firms into a network is how the province claims its share of the national tech boom.

headlines.headline: BCG Report: NZ Data-Centre Boom Could Be Worth $120 Billion — With 3,500 Construction Jobs Up For Grabs
headlines.byline: 23 August 2026 · National data-centre push and its trades boom — the electrical, mechanical and civil jobs on offer, and why Hawke's Bay should be paying attention
headlines.brief:
A new report from Boston Consulting Group (BCG) has sharply lifted New Zealand's growth story for data centres. The report by Boston Consulting Group (BCG) said New Zealand could capture up to $120 billion in economic activity from new data centres over the next decade if it moved quickly. That's a big jump — up from the group's earlier forecast of $70 billion in potential economic gains — and it's built on a larger future data centre build-out of 1 gigawatt (GW).

The jobs numbers are just as striking. BCG said a construction programme of that scale could drive economic activity across the country's supply chain, creating about 3500 jobs during the peak construction period, with about 60 percent of those roles expected to be in electrical and mechanical trades, and civil trades accounting for a further 21 percent. Once built, the report said that once operational, data centres typically sustain about one role for every megawatt of capacity, resulting in about 1000 ongoing jobs. BCG New Zealand managing director and partner Kelly Newton said "Between New Zealand's natural advantages, renewables development, stable political environment, and growing investor interest, it has the opportunity to move quickly to capture its slice of the global data centre pie, worth approximately $120 billion in economic activity."

The forecast lands as real projects start moving: Contact Energy announced it was exploring plans with CDC Data Centres for a potential large-scale 250-megawatt data centre at Stratford in Taranaki, while in the south, Datagrid is preparing to build a large-scale data centre at Makarewa, north of Invercargill. It's not uncontested — large builds have faced local opposition in the United States and the Greens have recently called for a one-year moratorium on data centre construction here.
headlines.lens: None of this build-out is landing in Hawke's Bay yet — the projects named are in Taranaki and Southland, not here — but the workforce mix BCG describes is the region's bread and butter: electricians, mechanical fitters and civil contractors are exactly the trades Hawke's Bay's ITOs and polytechs already train for orchards, wineries and post-Cyclone Gabrielle rebuild work. If a genuine gigawatt-scale national build-out arrives, the honest opportunity for the Bay isn't hosting a hyperscale campus — that will chase cheap land, grid capacity and renewable generation elsewhere — it's supplying skilled trades labour and components into a construction pipeline that BCG says will peak nationally within the decade. The region's economic development agencies and training providers should be watching where the actual consented projects land and making sure local apprentices and contractors are visible and ready to bid into that supply chain, rather than assuming a data centre itself is coming to Napier or Hastings.

headlines.headline: NZ's Venture-Backed Tech Firms Now Worth $133 Billion — But Is the Country Keeping the Gains?
headlines.byline: National · 18 Aug 2026 · A landmark valuation of NZ's startup economy, and a warning about where the benefits actually land
headlines.brief:
New Zealand's technology sector has received some unusually good news. A new report by global data platform Dealroom and NZ Growth Capital Partners estimates the combined enterprise value of New Zealand's venture-backed companies at NZ$133 billion. It identifies more than 400 firms, including eight "unicorns" that have reached a valuation or exit of more than US$1 billion. Two of these are "decacorns" valued at more than US$10 billion – aerospace firm Rocket Lab and global financial services provider FNZ. Relative to peer innovation economies, New Zealand generates unusually high enterprise value relative to the venture capital invested, an analysis of the report by University of Auckland Business School entrepreneurship professor Rod McNaughton notes. Even so, despite its high capital efficiency, New Zealand has less venture capital-backed enterprise value per person than several comparable innovation economies.

But the report's real sting is in the question it raises rather than the number it produces. Is New Zealand as good at retaining the wider economic benefits of successful technology companies as it is at creating them? A company can remain headquartered in New Zealand while its economic centre of gravity progressively moves elsewhere. Equally, a company can establish its headquarters offshore while retaining substantial research, engineering and other high-value activities in New Zealand.

Successful firms such as Xero, Trade Me, Pushpay and Rocket Lab produce experienced managers, engineers and investors who have learned how to build at a global scale. That is why the report describes Kiwi founders building major companies offshore as a "double loss" — New Zealand can miss both some of the original value creation and the subsequent recycling of talent and capital that helps produce the next generation of companies. Innovation policy should therefore pay as much attention to the productive capability successful firms leave behind as it does to capital invested, company valuations and unicorn counts. Ultimately, the greatest value of a successful technology company may be the capability it leaves behind. That is what makes the next success more likely.
headlines.lens: There's no Hawke's Bay unicorn in this report, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise — the region doesn't feature in it. But the argument at the heart of the piece is one the Bay should take personally: value isn't just what a company is worth at exit, it's whether the engineers, managers and technical know-how it trained stick around afterwards. For a region without a Rocket Lab or an FNZ, the practical takeaway isn't chasing unicorns — it's making sure that when Bay-connected people do cut their teeth at Auckland or Wellington scale-ups, or when a promising local software or agritech venture gets acquired, there's a reason for that experience and capability to come home rather than simply cash out and relocate. That means local firms and regional business support networks investing in retention — flexible remote-work arrangements, local advisory roles for returning talent, and visible pathways for founders who want to build from the regions rather than only from the main centres. It's a slower, less headline-grabbing strategy than landing a defence contract, but the report's own argument is that capability, not capital alone, is what compounds.

headlines.headline: Kiwi Workshops in the Running as Defence Opens Up to Homegrown Drones
headlines.byline: 17-18 Aug 2026 · No Bay firm named yet — but a $100m-$300m supply chain is opening up
headlines.brief:
New Zealand's drone-manufacturing world got a rare public airing this week when RNZ's The Detail visited Obsidian Systems, a workshop run by Philip Solaris at the end of a winding, gravel road in the far north of Auckland - overlooking a valley of native bush, and beyond to Hauturu in the Hauraki Gulf. Solaris, chief executive of the firm, says "We like to think of ourselves as the Skunk Works of robots", a nod to Lockheed Martin's secretive innovation arm. The piece is an insight into the world of drones and their makers, how they're used in conservation and disasters, and what our defence force plans to do with them, and it landed just as the Defence Force signalled real openings for local manufacturers.

Last month, the government announced it is starting the process to purchase long-range one-way strike drones, with the aim to review, trial and select a strike drone by the end of March next year. Defence is separately doing market research this week on unarmed long-range uncrewed aircraft systems that can conduct maritime surveillance tasks, starting with a request for information from businesses. Asked how the strike drones will be used, the Defence Force said that would "depend on a number of factors such as manufacturing, delivery, integration of various sub-systems and the time to train NZDF personnel to operate the new drones". Then-minister Chris Penk said both investments have $100 million to $300 million allocated, and Solaris — who has worked on robotic systems for nearly two decades — says New Zealand companies like his are capable of filling the orders for drones. "I believe all the capability is within New Zealand to be world leaders in this realm, I really do, I've seen it," he says, adding "it's not just our company, there's a whole lot of companies in New Zealand that can all be part of that" — noting "we can't manufacture huge frigates but we can manufacture thousands of small craft".

The scale of the wider opportunity is backed by industry figures: a Deloitte study commissioned by MBIE in April 2025 found New Zealand's advanced aviation sector generated $0.53 billion in revenue in FY2024 and directly supported 2,000 full-time jobs.
headlines.lens: No Hawke's Bay company gets a mention in any of this — and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. What's real is the shape of the opportunity: a defence budget line worth $100 million to $300 million for long-range strike drones, a parallel maritime-surveillance programme out for market research, and a Defence Force openly saying it wants to know what local manufacturers can build, deliver and integrate. That's a door, not a guarantee, and by Solaris's own account it favours a scattered field of small workshops rather than one or two big primes. If the Bay has precision engineering, composites, electronics or aviation-adjacent firms with the discipline to meet defence-grade standards, the sensible move now is simply to find the current RFI and put a submission in — not to wait for a press release confirming Napier or Hastings already has a seat at the table, because right now it doesn't.

headlines.headline: NZ's Tech Sector Now Worth $133 Billion — But Is the Bay Sharing the Upside?
headlines.byline: National · what a $133b tech stocktake — anchored by Rocket Lab's Māhia pad — means for the Bay
headlines.brief:
New Zealand's technology sector has been handed some strikingly good numbers. A new report by global data platform Dealroom and NZ Growth Capital Partners estimates the combined enterprise value of New Zealand's venture-backed companies at NZ$133 billion. The report identifies more than 400 firms, including eight "unicorns" that have reached a valuation or exit of more than US$1 billion, and two of these are "decacorns" valued at more than US$10 billion — aerospace firm Rocket Lab and global financial services provider FNZ, according to University of Auckland entrepreneurship professor Rod McNaughton, writing for The Conversation and republished by RNZ.

The standout finding isn't just the headline number — it's the efficiency behind it. As McNaughton notes, relative to peer innovation economies, New Zealand generates unusually high enterprise value relative to the venture capital invested, suggesting Kiwi founders are punching well above the size of the capital pool backing them. But the report also flags a leakage problem: Dealroom's definition includes companies founded here that subsequently moved overseas, and it identifies more than ten billion-dollar businesses created by Kiwi founders but built offshore, across software, fintech, artificial intelligence and consumer technology — a pattern the report frames as a "double loss" for New Zealand.

McNaughton's core argument is that raw valuation numbers understate the real prize. He writes that the economic value of a successful start-up lies not only in the company it becomes, but also in the companies, capabilities and capital that come after it, since successful firms produce experienced managers, engineers and investors who have learned how to build at a global scale — a cycle the report says is already occurring around companies like Xero, Trade Me, Pushpay and Rocket Lab.
headlines.lens: For Hawke's Bay, the headline decacorn in this national stocktake isn't some faceless Auckland software firm — it's Rocket Lab, whose Launch Complex 1 sits on Māhia. The site's launch operations are overseen by Luke Smith, who works on land his own Māori ancestors have called home, and who has spoken publicly about what it means to manage a launch complex in a place his whānau has always belonged to. That's a direct, tangible line from a $133 billion national number to a real job, a real whānau connection and real prestige happening on Bay soil. The lens McNaughton offers — that the real prize isn't the valuation but the capability, talent and capital a company leaves behind — is exactly the test the region should apply to Rocket Lab's presence: is Māhia and wider Hawke's Bay building a genuine bench of aerospace, engineering and technician skills that outlasts any single company, or is the Bay simply hosting infrastructure while the value accrues elsewhere? Realistically, the region can do relatively little to shape national venture capital flows or stop founders chasing offshore capital — that's a Wellington and Auckland policy conversation. What Hawke's Bay can and should do is the local, practical version of McNaughton's "capability" argument: back local training pipelines, apprenticeships and supplier contracts tied to the Māhia site, so that whatever happens to Rocket Lab's valuation, the skills and community ties it seeds stay rooted here.

headlines.headline: Māhia's Launch Pad Faces High Court Fight Over Gaza Spy Satellites
headlines.byline: Wellington High Court · a judicial review over BlackSky launches puts Māhia's mana whenua on the record
headlines.brief:
Three New Zealand citizens have taken the Government to the High Court at Wellington over Rocket Lab's Māhia launch site — this time not about money, but about who those rockets are arming. Yasser Abdulaal, Maher Nazzal and Dr Timoti Te Moke have filed proceedings seeking a judicial review of the Government's approval of Rocket Lab's BlackSky satellite launches at Māhia, with the application backed by the Palestine Solidarity Network Aotearoa (PSNA). The applicants say the satellite launches risked supplying Israel's military with targeting data to use in Gaza, and they want the courts to intervene before more go up.

The case challenges former Space Minister Judith Collins' approval of four launches, and is also aimed at current Space Minister Chris Penk, who in April approved a further 26 BlackSky launches the plaintiffs are trying to stop. The pleadings are laid under the Outer Space and High-altitude Activities Act 2017. PSNA says it raised its concerns about Israeli military use of BlackSky satellites with Collins in November 2024, after Collins and MBIE had already granted BlackSky's payload permit in December 2023 without, in PSNA's telling, questioning whether the Israeli military was a current end-user of the satellites. PSNA spokeswoman Rinad Tamimi called the ministry's approach "wilful ignorance", saying Collins refused all PSNA requests to reconsider her approval.

Crucially, this isn't only a Wellington argument — it has a Māhia voice. Sonya Smith, an uri of Māhia iwi Rongomaiwahine and neighbouring Nūhaka iwi Ngāti Rākaipaaka, said mana whenua had real concerns about BlackSky and the direction of the Government, describing the use of ancestral whenua for satellite launches marketed to defence and intelligence agencies, without meaningful engagement with tangata whenua or regard for wāhi tapu, as a Treaty failure and a moral failure.
headlines.lens: Whatever the court decides, this case puts a distinct kind of pressure on the pad that anchors Hawke's Bay's place in the global space economy — not a commercial question this time, but a legal and moral one that goes to the heart of who Māhia's iwi are, and were, consulted with before rockets carrying foreign payloads leave their whenua. The region has real standing here through Rongomaiwahine and neighbouring Ngāti Rākaipaaka, whose representative has now put mana whenua's unease on the public record, and that's a voice Hawke's Bay institutions — the regional council, Wairoa District Council, and iwi bodies — should be listening to directly rather than leaving the conversation to Wellington lawyers and Auckland advocacy groups. There's little the Bay can or should do to influence the litigation itself; judicial review of ministerial decisions under the Outer Space and High-altitude Activities Act is squarely a national legal and foreign-policy matter. But the region can insist on better local engagement processes for future payload approvals at Māhia, and treat this as a reminder that hosting strategic space infrastructure carries reputational and cultural exposure alongside its economic upside.

headlines.headline: Rocket Lab, Xero and Air NZ Shed $90 Billion in Value — With Māhia's Launch Pad in the Middle of It
headlines.byline: National markets · what a share-market wobble at Rocket Lab means for the region hosting its launch site
headlines.brief:
Three of New Zealand's biggest-name listed companies have had a brutal year on the markets. Rocket Lab, Xero and Air New Zealand have lost a combined $90bn in share value this year, despite all three having strong brands and growing revenue. Rocket Lab — the aerospace company that launches its Electron rockets from Māhia, on the Hawke's Bay coast, and is the most widely held stock among Sharesies investors — is down 55% since May. Air New Zealand, the second most widely held stock on Sharesies, is down 25% since February, continuing a 56% decline since 2021. Xero, the Wellington-based accounting software company, is down 62% from its June 2025 high.

The downturn began on February 3, 2026, when roughly $NZ485bn of market cap was wiped out in a single day from software and financial services stocks — a rout a Jefferies trader dubbed the "SaaSpocalypse", a term that has since caught on with Wall Street. It isn't just institutional investors feeling it — hundreds of thousands of other New Zealanders have small holdings in these three companies through their KiwiSavers, especially in Air New Zealand, the only of the three currently listed on the NZX. Analysts say the declines can partly be attributed to company-specific management decisions but are more broadly the result of global forces wreaking havoc on their particular industry sectors. Morningstar's Roy van Keulen has argued Xero has become "materially undervalued" despite its dominant market share in New Zealand and Australia.

Rocket Lab's pullback looks less alarming in context: even after losing over half its market cap from its peak, the company is still up 67% over the last 12 months. Between May 2024 and May 2026 its stock ran from US$4 a share to a high of $143.48 — a 3,487% return for anyone who timed the top perfectly, or a still-hefty 1,762% for those who held on. Analysts caution a pullback like this isn't unusual after such a run, for a speculative company that is still yet to turn a profit — but real concerns remain.
headlines.lens: This is a market story, not a Hawke's Bay story — but it has a physical address here. Rocket Lab's rockets don't just make headlines in Auckland boardrooms; they lift off from Māhia, meaning Wairoa and the wider Bay carry real exposure to a company whose share price has fallen 55% since May, however comfortable its 67% twelve-month return still looks. The honest lens is caution rather than alarm: nothing in this reporting suggests Māhia launch cadence, local jobs or contractor spend has actually been cut — the volatility so far is a listed-market story about valuation, not a confirmed operational pullback at the launch site. What the region can sensibly do is keep an eye on it: local suppliers and contractors tied to the Māhia pad should treat a single company's share-price cycle as a reminder not to over-concentrate around one customer, and anyone with KiwiSaver exposure should recognise, as hundreds of thousands of other New Zealanders now are, that a chunk of their retirement savings rides on names like Rocket Lab and Air New Zealand. Beyond watching the numbers and diversifying where it can, there's little for Hawke's Bay to actively do here — this is a national capital-markets moment playing out on a launch pad the Bay happens to host, not a regional crisis to respond to.

headlines.headline: Hastings Robot-Maker Can't Build Fast Enough as US Apple Industry Buys Up Hawke's Bay AI Packers
headlines.byline: Hastings · a homegrown robotics exporter shows what Hawke's Bay tech can look like at scale
headlines.brief:
A Hawke's Bay robotics manufacturer is being run off its feet by demand from across the Pacific. Hawk Technology builds its apple-packing robots in Hastings and ships them to the US, where apple packhouses in Washington are lining up to get them. General manager Sam Combs told RNZ it had built a few hundred machines for the New Zealand market over the past few years, and now the US market is really taking off. The first 50 Gen 5 Apple Packers are running in Washington, with another 250 on order — a market Combs says is "about seven times the size of New Zealand for apples only. Washington's the Hawke's Bay equivalent of New Zealand and grows about two-thirds of the fruit." Demand, he says, is now "greater than our manufacturing capability."

The company's roots are in packaging, not robotics: the Comb family bought Hawk Packaging and began turning the recycling into the cardboard trays that sit between layers of fruit when it's boxed up in packhouses. Customers began asking if the tray-handling itself could be automated, leading first to a Tray Denester, then a Tray Inserter, and eventually to the third product that's been the most popular – the Robotic Apple Packer, which now uses 15 AI cameras working simultaneously to inspect fruit for flaws and sort it by colour and quality into trays.

The growth has been rapid: seven years ago Hawk Technology had just two research design and development staff, which has grown to a team of over 50 workers to keep up with the growing demand for robotics. Senior mechatronics engineer Ben Kloosterman, who works on the Gen 5 Apple Packer, said previously with industrial automation it was always a bit frustrating cause the technology was like 20 years behind, so being free to learn and grow in that cutting edge technology is really really cool. Combs said the next target is stone fruit — "an obvious kind of next cab off the ranks. We'll be looking into that over the next year or so," he said.

Crucially, the whole operation stays local: Combs said the company has a full design team in-house, fabrication in-house, and electricals in-house, because "a big philosophy of ours is just keeping everything here. We didn't want to have to send stuff overseas," he said. And while the robots are replacing some packhouse workers, Combs said for many employers it's solved a labour shortage problem: "In New Zealand it was a real problem for our customers to even find that labour in the first place, so it's there to complement their existing workforces," he said. Alan McDonald from the Employers and Manufacturers Association agreed, saying while there's been an increase in workplaces using AI and robots, it hadn't resulted in fewer jobs overall.
headlines.lens: This is the story hawkesbay.tech should be proudest of running, because it isn't a national policy story with a regional footnote — it's a Hastings company beating the world at something hard, on its own turf. Hawk Technology's growth from a two-person R&D shop, born out of a family packaging business, into a 50-plus-strong robotics team exporting AI-vision packing machines to an American market seven times our size, is proof that world-class mechatronics and software talent can be built and kept in the Bay rather than lost to Auckland or overseas. The region's job now is to protect and multiply that: backing local training pipelines in mechatronics, machine vision and embedded software (through EIT, Hi-Tech Hawke's Bay and schools) so Hawk Technology and its planned stone-fruit expansion can hire locally rather than poach nationally; helping other Bay packhouses and growers navigate the labour-shortage-versus-job-displacement tension Combs himself flagged, and which the Employers and Manufacturers Association says hasn't yet cost jobs overall; and using Hawk Technology as the flagship case study when pitching Hawke's Bay to investors and skilled migrants as a place where deep-tech manufacturing, not just orchards, actually happens.

headlines.headline: Government Cashes In Chorus Fibre Loans Early for $702m
headlines.byline: Wellington · what a broadband debt sale means for Hawke's Bay's fibre and infrastructure funding
headlines.brief:
The Government has struck a deal to get its money out of Chorus early. Finance Minister Nicola Willis and Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop confirmed the Crown has entered into binding agreements to monetise the debt it holds in telecommunications lines company Chorus, with Willis saying the transaction delivers net proceeds to the Crown of approximately $702 million against a book value of $642 million — "a strong commercial result representing a gain over book value of over $60 million."

Between 2012 and 2023 the Government provided $1.336 billion in interest-free loans to Chorus to help finance and accelerate the roll-out of fibre broadband across New Zealand, and Chorus repaid $170 million of that funding in 2025. "The fibre rollout is now complete and has delivered enormous benefits for New Zealanders, with most people now able to connect seamlessly with family, friends, and colleagues across the country and around the world," Willis said. The loans were not due to be fully repaid until 2036, but after testing the market, the Government has decided to get the present value of its money back sooner so it can be invested elsewhere — the alternative would be to wait another five to 10 years for Chorus to repay the Crown. The deal also appears to include some form of limited investor protection through NIFFCo, or National Infrastructure Funding and Financing Limited, a Crown-owned company set up as the government's shopfront for private capital investment in public infrastructure, though the government has not disclosed the nature, scale, or potential Crown exposure involved. Crucially, the transaction does not change the ownership of Chorus, or the services and assets it provides or owns.

Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop says the funds received through this process will be ring-fenced and redeployed into Budget 2026 to help fund other projects. Willis said the proceeds had been anticipated in Budget 2026, which she said meant it could fund more infrastructure, including roads, hospital upgrades and classrooms, though she did not say the money would be specifically earmarked for those projects. Settlement is expected to occur in August 2026. Chorus acknowledged the Government's announcement on the New Zealand stock exchange (NZX), where its ordinary shares trade at $9.62 each and the company's market capitalisation is $4.17 billion.
headlines.lens: This is a Wellington balance-sheet story, not a new cable in the ground for Hawke's Bay — the fibre rollout that these loans funded is, as Willis herself put it, already complete and has delivered benefits for New Zealanders connecting with family, friends and colleagues nationwide, so there's no fresh connectivity announcement for the region here. What matters locally is the money's next stop: Bishop says the funds will be ring-fenced and redeployed into Budget 2026 to help fund infrastructure, and Willis floated roads, hospital upgrades and classrooms as candidates without committing any of it to specific projects. Hawke's Bay's honest play is to watch the Budget process closely and make its case loudly — for state highway resilience, for hospital capacity, for school upgrades — because this is genuinely uncommitted capital being freed up, not a regional allocation already decided. There's little else the Bay can or should do beyond that lobbying; this is a financing manoeuvre in Wellington, and pretending it's a local infrastructure win before the Budget confirms where the $702m actually lands would be getting ahead of the facts.

headlines.headline: NZ Court AI Guidelines Unchanged Since 2023 as Academics Flag 'Agentic AI' Gap
headlines.byline: National · late July 2026 · what unrevised AI court guidance means for Hawke's Bay's lawyers and litigants
headlines.brief:
New Zealand's judiciary is facing calls from some legal academics to update its rules on generative AI use in courtrooms, though not everyone in the profession agrees an overhaul is urgent. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) use in New Zealand's legal system is continuing to increase, a fact the Office of the Chief Justice has acknowledged, but the judiciary's guidelines for AI use were last updated in 2023.

University of Auckland Law School lecturer Matt Bartlett said other judiciaries around the world were updating their guidance far more frequently than New Zealand, saying "they're out of step with the capabilities, the risk profile, and frankly the practice overseas." Bartlett also noted AI use typically did not need to be disclosed, which he said made it difficult to understand the extent to which AI was already influencing the justice system. Fellow senior lecturer Dr Joshua Yuvaraj argued the technology was evolving so quickly that the guidelines should be reviewed regularly to ensure they remained fit for purpose.

Yuvaraj's concern isn't just chatbots drafting documents. Technology, he said, had moved beyond just generative AI technologies to agentic AI, where AI systems could automate tasks such as organising workflows, responding to emails and other administrative work, developments he said warranted some attention in the court's guidelines. He also wanted to see continual emphasis on the privacy and confidentiality risks associated with using AI tools.

Not everyone thinks the rules need rewriting, however. Auckland barrister Josh McBride said while the guidelines were now a few years old, they had largely stood the test of time, saying "I've looked at them recently, and in fairness, they do a pretty good job." McBride did not believe AI use should necessarily have to be disclosed, though he had seen instances where litigants armed with AI tools were producing disproportionate volumes of AI generated material for what the case entailed, and said there was a benefit in clearer rules on the volume of AI-generated material people could file and clearer warnings that litigants were responsible for verifying anything AI produced before submitting it to the court. For its part, a spokesperson from the Office of the Chief Justice said the judiciary recognised the opportunities created by AI to support access to justice and the timely, efficient and proportionate administration of justice, but it was taking a cautious approach to the exploration and adoption of Generative AI to support the work of the courts.
headlines.lens: There's no Rocket-Lab-sized dollar figure here, and honestly Hawke's Bay has little direct lever to pull on national court policy — that sits with the Chief Justice's office and the judiciary's own advisory processes, not regional government. But the region does have real skin in this game: our district and High Court sittings in Napier and Hastings, local law firms, Community Law Hawke's Bay, and self-represented litigants are all already living with whatever informal AI practice has grown since the 2023 guidelines were issued, debate about updating them or not. The honest, useful response for the Bay isn't a moonshot — it's plumbing. Local firms and the Hawke's Bay District Law Society could use this moment to run a plain-English session on what's actually permitted when a solicitor or a litigant in person uses ChatGPT-style tools to draft an affidavit or chase case law, rather than waiting for Wellington to settle the Bartlett-versus-McBride debate about whether the rules need a rewrite or just better enforcement. If agentic AI is now quietly triaging emails and workflows inside firms here too, the region's legal community has as much reason as any to watch closely, and weigh in, on whatever the Office of the Chief Justice does next, because whatever rule finally lands will apply just as much in a Hastings courtroom as in Auckland's.

headlines.headline: Rocket Lab wins record US$266m US Space Force contract — with its home pad still at Māhia
headlines.byline: National · what a record defence deal means for the region that hosts Rocket Lab's launch site
headlines.brief:
Rocket Lab has secured the largest contract in its history: a US$266 million (about NZ$460 million) award from the United States Space Force's Space Systems Command Rocket Systems Launch Program. The deal covers 12 guaranteed suborbital launches, with options for up to six more, flown on the company's HASTE rocket — a suborbital variant of its Electron — to support US missile-defence testing.

The first flight is expected no earlier than the end of 2026, and launches will run primarily from Rocket Lab's pad at the Pacific Spaceport Complex on Kodiak Island, Alaska. Founder and chief executive Sir Peter Beck said the contract's size reflects the Space Force's confidence in the company's ability to deliver with speed and scale. Rocket Lab shares rose almost 5% on the news.
headlines.lens: Rocket Lab is New Zealand's flagship space company, founded in Auckland in 2006, and its only operational launch site is Launch Complex 1 at Māhia Peninsula in the Wairoa district of Hawke's Bay. The honest picture is that these HASTE launches will fly from Alaska, not Māhia, so the immediate jobs and activity land offshore. But the deal cements Rocket Lab's trajectory and keeps Māhia on the map as the home of a company now trusted with US national-security work. For the Bay, the opportunity is upstream and long-term: a serious STEM and aerospace-skills pipeline through EIT and local schools so Wairoa and wider Hawke's Bay young people can move into the sector; supplier and services links to Rocket Lab's operations; and Wairoa economic-development planning that treats the launch site as an anchor asset rather than a curiosity. The region should be deliberate about capturing the spillover, because the marquee contracts themselves will keep going where the launch pads and customers are.

headlines.headline: Auckland's mayor is spending 100 days — and 100 t-shirts — championing the city's startups
headlines.byline: Auckland · what the city's 100-day startup push means for the Bay
headlines.brief:
Auckland mayor Wayne Brown has launched 100 Days of Start-ups, wearing a different local startup's branded t-shirt every day for 100 days from 3 July to spotlight the city's founders. The campaign builds toward Auckland Startup Week (12–16 October 2026), with the full programme due to launch on 5 August, and is backed by Auckland Council's Economic Development Office, the Auckland Technology and Innovation Alliance and the New Zealand Institute for Advanced Technology.

More than a quarter of the 100 featured startups are tied to the University of Auckland — whose Centre for Innovation and Entrepreneurship says its alumni have raised more than $8.2 billion in capital over 23 years — with early names including retail-crime intelligence firm Auror and medical-device maker Kitea Health. “By wearing these shirts, I want to draw attention to the talent we have right here in our city,” Brown said, arguing Auckland is “punching well above our weight in deep tech, heavy industry disruption and pure Kiwi ingenuity.”
headlines.lens: For Hawke's Bay the interesting part isn't the t-shirts — it's how cheap and effective a bit of civic visibility can be for a startup scene. Auckland already has the capital and the density; the Bay has a real but scattered base of around 500 tech firms and the Hi-Tech Hawke's Bay network, and almost none of the national spotlight. The region could borrow the playbook directly: a low-cost, high-visibility local campaign — the mayors, the port, big employers and EIT actively championing named Bay startups — that turns a loose scene into a story investors and talent can follow. The more concrete move is to plug in rather than compete: get Bay founders and university-linked ventures onto the Auckland Startup Week stage in October, where the capital and networks actually are, and use it to pull investment and profile back to the region. Auckland is showing that celebrating startups is a deliberate choice a city makes; the honest question for Hawke's Bay is whether it will make the same choice or keep its best stories to itself.

headlines.headline: NZ tech is now a $20bn sector — and almost all of it sits in two cities
headlines.byline: National · what the country’s tech boom means for the regions
headlines.brief:
New Zealand’s top 200 tech firms turned over $20 billion last year, with tech exports up 12.4% to $15.31 billion — cementing the sector as the country’s third-largest export earner after dairy and tourism, according to the 2025 TIN report. High-tech manufacturing ($9.8 billion) and ICT ($8.93 billion) led the way, and 40 firms now clear $100 million in revenue, up from 19 a decade ago.

But the growth is lopsided. Auckland ($10.5b) and Wellington ($5.2b) account for the vast majority of that revenue, leaving the rest of the country to share what’s left. And over the past decade these firms have added offshore jobs about three times faster than domestic ones. The value is compounding — just not where most of the country lives.
headlines.lens: The country’s tech wealth is real and compounding — but it’s pooling in Auckland and Wellington while those same firms add jobs offshore faster than they do at home. That gap is precisely where a region like Hawke’s Bay can step in. The Bay can’t out-scale the main centres, and shouldn’t try to; what it can do is compete for the work leaking out of them. It has a lower cost base, the lifestyle pull that now moves remote tech workers, and a primary-sector economy — orchards, wineries, packhouses, the port — that throws off real software problems worth solving. The honest catch is that none of this happens by default. It takes deliberate choices: fast, affordable connectivity and housing, visible pathways from local schools and STEM programmes into tech careers, and employers willing to hire and train juniors here rather than import finished talent. The Bay’s opportunity isn’t to beat Auckland — it’s to become the obvious place the overflow lands.
